newsitem.title: USA: New guidelines issued for child urinary disorder.
newsitem.headline: New guidelines issued for child urinary disorder.

text.p: The leading U.S. urological group Monday released treatment guidelines urging use of low-dose antibiotics for a urinary problem that affects one out of every 100 children.

At its annual meeting in New Orleans, the American Urological Association recommended long-term use of antibiotics instead of surgery, which had been initially recommended. Surgery would be an option in severe cases or if the drugs did not work.

Vesicoureteral reflux is a urinary problem that occurs when children are born with a defect in the attachment between the ureter and bladder. It causes urine to back up from the bladder into the kidney, and can lead to kidney infections, which can have more serious implications later in life.
The disorder is not painful and is usually diagnosed when the child is 2 or 3 years old and develops a urinary tract infection.

"There is disagreement about the optimal management of this disorder, even among specialists caring for these children," said the association's president Dr. Jack McAninch of the University of California, San Francisco. A panel of experts was convened to develop guidelines.

Dr. Jack Elder of the Rainbow Babies and Childrens Hospital in Cleveland, who headed the panel, said in a telephone interview that children should be on a low dose of antibiotics to ward off infection. They should be monitored every one to two years.
In many cases, the condition will clear up or improve greatly. In more severe or persistent cases, surgery may be required.

"The medications that we recommend for this are very safe, they've been around for 15-20 years," Elder said. He said if the drugs were taken in low doses there was not a threat of resistance to antibiotics.
